en: To conclude this module, we'll have a look
at another very important aspect and that
would be testing, specifically unit testing.
Of course, you should be testing your code.
So that means you should be running
automated tests and it would be even better
if you would write your code in a
test-driven way.
This course is not about testing or
test-driven development though.
But unit testing will indeed help you not
just with writing
error-free code but also with writing clean
code.
Because there's one simple question which
you automatically have to answer when you
utilize testing.
Can you easily test a function?
If the answer to this is yes,
if you're not having any problems with side
effects like data being written to a
database, which you typically don't want
during testing,
and if you don't do 10 different things in
one function, which are then therefore
difficult to test,
then it's great and you probably have clean
code.
If the answer is no though, if you find that
one function does too many things and you
therefore have to write many tests testing
different things for one and the same
function, or if you have a lot of side
effects in there,
then you might wanna consider splitting up
your function so that you have multiple
functions which are then easier to test.
And that is how unit testing will help you
write cleaner code and especially will help
you write slim and focused functions because
it turns out that small functions which only
do one thing and which don't have unexpected
side effects are way easier to test than big
functions.
Now, as an example, here's another dummy
function, addProduct.
It's validating some input, showing an error
message, and then creating and storing a
product. And therefore, of course, it's very
similar to the createUser example you saw
earlier in this module.
Now, obviously, we can immediately see by
now that we have mixed levels of abstraction
here and that the distance between the level
of abstraction of the function name and the
level of abstraction of certain steps in
that function is too big.
But even if we wouldn't see that, we would
face problems when we try to write tests for
this function.
Here are 2
dummy tests
as we could write them in JavaScript, for
example. And of course, no matter which
programming language you use, your tests
will look something like this.
I got 2 test cases here
and in the first case, I test whether the
overall creation of the product works.
In the second case, I'm actually only
interested in the ID and I wanna find out if
the ID was generated correctly
because it turns out that my ID
should be composed of both the name of the
product as well as some random number which
is converted to a string.
Now when writing these tests, I can see and
feel that something's wrong with my
addProduct function.
Because for one, we have an unwanted side
effect, not an unexpected one, but an
unwanted one during testing. We are writing
a product to the database.
In addition, if I'm just interested in
testing whether the ID was created
correctly, I still have to run the entire
addProduct function including that unwanted
side effect just to then find out whether
the ID was generated correctly or not.
So therefore this clearly signals to us that
something's wrong with the function.
We could test more, for example if
validation fails.
For that we would need to check whether this
function completes successfully or not.
And all these tests would run on the same
function testing totally different things.
So clearly this is not a great function. We
should split it up so that we have multiple
functions which are then easier to test.
This is how we could refactor this
addProduct function to be cleaner.
It's way shorter and it's split up into
multiple smaller pieces.
I have the validateProductData function
which throws an error if we have invalid
input.
And even that is split up further into the
inputIsValid function and then the reusable
isEmpty and hasMinValue functions here.
And the advantage of this is that I now, for
example, can write tests which only test the
isEmpty function.
So I can only test this small unit now
and I can test parts of my validation or
also the entire validation if I wanted to
without running the entire addProduct
function.
I can also test just the generation of an ID
if I wanted to because I did extract an
extra function
for this
so I could check whether an ID is generated
correctly without creating an entire product
and storing that product in some database.
And that is why unit testing helps you with
writing cleaner code. You could derive this
code without unit testing as well,
but when writing tests and when testing
everything, which I don't do in this
solution, I just have some examples here,
but when testing everything,
you will automatically see what should be
extracted and what should not be extracted
because you wanna extract as much as
possible to write as many tests as possible,
as long as they make some sense, of course.
Now we don't need to write any unit test for
addProduct. We could write an integration
test for this, but we do have all these unit
tests which we can write for the small
extracted functions we have here.
That's why testing matters, not just for
avoiding errors and bugs, but also for
writing clean code.
